BEFORE THE NEW MEXICO PUBLIC REGULATION COMMISSION
IN THE MATTER OF SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC                         )
SERVICE COMPANY’S APPLICATION FOR: (1)                       )
REVISION OF ITS RETAIL RATES UNDER                           )
ADVICE NOTICE 341; AND (2) OTHER                             )
ASSOCIATED RELIEF.                                           )      CASE NO. 25-00079-UT
                                                             )
SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY,                         )
                                                             )
APPLICANT.                                                   )

      LOUSIANA ENERGY SERVICES' AND FEDERAL EXECUTIVE AGENCIES'
                     INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

        Intervenors Louisiana Energy Services, L.L.C. ("LES") and the Federal Executive

 Agencies ("FEA") hereby jointly submit to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

 ("Commission" or "NMPRC") their Initial Post-Hearing Brief pursuant to the Hearing Examiners'

 Order on Post-Hearing Briefing issued on July 28, 2026 and 1.2.2.36 NMAC.

        The primary focus of the hearing and post-hearing briefing is whether the Commission

 should approve the Comprehensive Stipulation ("Stipulation") that would resolve Southwestern

 Public Service Company's ("SPS" or "Company") rate case. SPS, LES, and FEA are all signatories

 to the Stipulation. The Stipulation was filed on June 22, 2026 following extensive negotiations in

 which all parties were invited to participate. The only party that opposes any portion of the

 Stipulation is the Commission's Utility Division Staff ("Staff"). All other parties either joined the

 Stipulation or do not oppose it.

        The Commission should approve the Stipulation because the evidence demonstrates that it

 is the result of serious bargaining between knowledgeable entities, including the utility and its

 customers who will bear the burden of the rate increase; balances the interests of ratepayers and

 the utility; is consistent with well-established regulatory principles; complies with NM law; is in
 the public interest; and will result in fair, just and reasonable rates. The Stipulation is fair, just and

reasonable and should be approved.

I.        Legal Standards

          A.     Rates Must Be Just and Reasonable

          The Public Utility Act ("PUA") requires that public utility rates be just and reasonable.1

“To set a just and reasonable rate, the Commission must balance the investor’s interest against the

ratepayer’s interest.”2 In reaching its ultimate decision, the Commission is not tied down either by

the PUA or by case law to considering only a single factor in establishing rates. The New Mexico

Supreme Court has “consistently construed the [PUA] broadly rather than to limit the Commission

to any one particular method [of ratemaking]; the touchstone is the reasonableness of the ultimate

decision.”3

          When setting rates, it is the end result reached and not the method employed that is

controlling.4 Since at least 1950, when the New Mexico Supreme Court expressly cited with

approval the standards enunciated in Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co.,5 those

standards have governed New Mexico‘s regulation of utilities.6 In Hope, the United States

Supreme Court stated:


1
  Sections 62-8-1 and 62-8-7 of the PUA provides that rates must be "just and reasonable." Sections 62-3-
1.B of the PUA declares the policy of the state that the public interest, the interest of consumers and the
interest of investors require the regulation and supervision of public utilities to the end that reasonable and
proper services shall be available at "fair, just and reasonable rates." The PUA does not offer any
distinction or clarification between the two terms.
2
    Behles v. New Mexico Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 1992-NMSC-047, ¶ 29, 114 N.M. 154.
3
    N.M. Industrial Energy Consumers v. N.M. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 1986-NMSC-059, ¶ 29, 104 N.M.
4
    Attorney General v. N.M. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 1991-NMSC-028, ¶ 26, 111 N.M. 636.
5
    Hope, 320 U.S. 591 (1944).
6
    N.M. v. Mountain States Tel. & Tel. Co., 1950-NMSC-055, 54 N.M. 315.

                                                      2
           Under the statutory standard of ‘just and reasonable’ it is the result reached, not the
          method employed, which is controlling. It is not the theory but the impact of the
          rate which counts. If the total effect of the rate order cannot be said to be unjust and
          unreasonable, judicial inquiry . . . is at an end. The fact that the method employed
          to reach the result may contain infirmities is not then important....

          The ratemaking process under the Act, i.e., the fixing of ‘just and reasonable’ rates,
          involves a balancing of the investor and the consumer interests. Thus, we stated in
          the Natural Gas Pipeline Co. case that ‘regulation does not insure that the business
          shall produce net revenues.’ 315 U.S. 590. But such considerations aside, the
          investor interest has a legitimate concern with the financial integrity of the company
          whose rates are being regulated. From the investor or company point of view it is
          important that there be enough revenue not only for operating expenses but also for
          the capital costs of the business. These include service on the debt and dividends
          on the stock.... By that standard the return to the equity owner should be
          commensurate with returns on investments in other enterprises having
          corresponding risks. That return, moreover, should be sufficient to assure
          confidence in the financial integrity of the enterprise, so as to maintain its credit
          and to attract capital.7

          Correlative to the “end result” test in determining whether rates are just and reasonable is

the “zone of reasonableness” test adopted by the New Mexico Supreme Court and the federal

courts after the announcement of that test in Federal Power Commission v. Natural Gas Pipeline

Co.8 As stated by the New Mexico Supreme Court, “[t[here is a zone of reasonableness between

[utility] confiscation and [ratepayer] extortion in which the Commission’s jurisdiction to make

rates should be confined.”9

          Therefore, under the PUA, the Commission has the two-fold obligation to determine that

the existing authorized rates are no longer just and reasonable and that the new rates proposed are

not unjust or otherwise contrary to law. There is no dispute in this case that the existing rates are




7
    Hope, 320 U.S. at 602-03 (citations omitted).
8
    Natural Gas Pipeline, 315 U.S. 575, 585 (1942).
9
    Mountain States Tel. & Tel., 1950-NMSC-055, ¶ 44, 54 N.M. 315.


                                                      3
 no longer just and reasonable. There is no evidence in the record in this case that the stipulated

rates are unjust or otherwise contrary to law. To the contrary, the record is replete with evidence

that supports the conclusion that the Stipulation will result in fair, just and reasonable rates and

should be approved.

          B.      Contested Stipulations

          The Commission has a well-established policy encouraging the filing of stipulations, and

it has adopted rules governing procedures to consider settlements negotiated by the parties.10 The

Commission has stated on numerous occasions that it favors “the settlement of disputes to avoid

costly and protracted litigation” and recognizes that “a cooperative approach may be more

effective in reconciling the interest of all the parties than would the polarization which often

accompanies adversarial proceedings.”11

          The proponents of a stipulation bear the burden of supporting the stipulation with sufficient

evidence and legal argument to allow the Commission to approve it. 12 Stipulations must be fair,

just, reasonable, and in the public interest.13 Additional criteria the Commission has applied in

evaluating the reasonableness of stipulations include:


10
     See Rule 1.2.2.20 NMAC.
11
  See, e.g., Application of Southwestern Public Service Company for Revision of its Retail Electric Rates
Pursuant to Advice Notice Nos. 217, 218, and 219 and Request for Expedited Interim Relief Authorizing
Recovery of Capacity Related Costs Associated with the New Hobbs Generating Station, Case No. 08-
00354-UT, Final Order Conditionally Approving Stipulation, at 12 (Jul. 14, 2009); see also Attorney
General v. Pub Serv. Comm’n, 1991-NMSC-028, ¶ 13, 111 N.M. 636, 640 (“a cooperative approach in
reconciling the interests of the parties was consistent with the public policy favoring settlement of
disputes.”).
12
     Rule 1.2.2.20(A) and (B) NMAC (uncontested stipulations and contested stipulations respectively).
13
  See Applications of Public Service Company of New Mexico and New Mexico Gas Company, Inc. for the
Abandonment, Purchase and Sale of Gas Utility Assets and Services, Case No. 08-00078-UT, Certification
of Stipulation (Nov. 24, 2008), at 3, Final Order Partially Approving Certification of Stipulation (Dec. 11,
2008).


                                                      4
                Is the settlement a product of serious bargaining among capable, knowledgeable

        parties?

               Does the settlement, as a whole, benefit customers and the public interest?

               Does the settlement, as a whole, violate any important regulatory principle or

        practice?14

        These questions can be restated as the following affirmative criteria or factors. The

proponent of the stipulation must demonstrate that:

        (1) the parties and Staff had notice and an opportunity to be heard on the stipulation,

        (2) the stipulation is in accordance with applicable law, and

        (3) a preponderance of the evidence in the record (as a whole) supports the Commission’s

conclusion that the stipulation is fair, just, reasonable, and in the public interest.15

        The Stipulation meets all of these criteria and should be approved.

        C.      Evidentiary Standard

        The rule in administrative proceedings in general, and adjudications before this

Commission in particular, is that unless a statute provides otherwise, the proponent of an order or

moving party has the burden of proof.16 The quantum of proof in administrative adjudications is,


14
  Suspension of a Portion of Gas Company of New Mexico’s Purchase Gas Adjustment Clause, and the
Investigation Relative Thereto, PUC Case No. 2453, Certification of Stipulation, at 11 (May 18, 1993); Re
Public Service Company of New Mexico, 110 P.U.R. 4th at 85 (quoting with approval In re Cleveland
Electric Illuminating Co., 99 P.U.R. 4th 407, 449 (Ohio PUC 1989)); Application of Southwestern Public
Service Co. for Revision of its Retail Rates Pursuant to Advice Notice Nos. 217, 218, and 219 et al., Case
No. 08-00354-UT, Final Order Conditionally Approving Stipulation at 13 (Jul. 14, 2009).
15
  In the Matter of Southwestern Public Service Company's Application for (1) Revision of its Retail Rates
Under Advice Notice No. 312; (2) Authority to Abandon its Plant X Unit 1, Plant X Unit 2, and Cunningham
Unit 1 Generating Stations and Amend the Abandonment Date of the Tolk Generating Station; and (3)
Other Associated Relief, Case No. 22-00286-UT, Certification of Stipulation (Sept. 6, 2023) at 33-34,
adopted by Final Order Adopting Certification of Stipulation (Oct. 19, 2023).
16
  3 DAVIS, KENNETH CULP, ADMINISTRATIVE LAW TREATISE § 16.9 at 255–57 (2d ed. 1980).
See Int’l Minerals and Chemical Corp. v. N.M. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 81 N.M. 280, 283, 466 P.2d 557, 560

                                                    5
 again unless expressly provided otherwise, a preponderance of record evidence. 17 Preponderance

of the evidence means the greater weight of the evidence (i.e., evidence that has more convincing

force).18 It has superior evidentiary weight that, though not sufficient to free the mind wholly from

all reasonable doubt, is still sufficient to incline a fair and impartial mind to one side of the issue

rather than the other.19

II.       The Stipulation Meets the Standards for Approval

          In this case, it is undisputed that all parties and Staff had notice and an opportunity to be

heard on the Stipulation. A public hearing was held on July 13 through 16, 2026, and Staff

presented its witnesses and cross-examined opposing witnesses. As reviewed below, there is

substantial evidence in the record that supports a conclusion that the Stipulation will result in fair,

just and reasonable rates and is in the public interest. The Stipulation was the product of serious

bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties, and results in fair, just and reasonable rates that

balance the interests of the utility and its ratepayers, and allocates costs across rate classes

according to well-established standards that appropriately applies the principles of gradualism.




(1970) (“Although the statute does not specifically place any burden of proof on [complainant]
International, the courts have uniformly imposed on administrative agencies the customary common-law
rule that the moving party has the burden of proof.”).
17

of the evidence”) (emphasis in original); see El Paso Electric Co. et al. v. N.M. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 1985-

evidence’ standard is customary in administrative and other civil proceedings.”); Re Southwestern Public
Service Co., Case No. 2678, Recommended Decision of the Hearing Examiner (Nov. 15, 1996) (“No matter
how the Commission describes its standard of review, SPS bears the burden of proof in this case. SPS must
demonstrate that a preponderance of evidence exists in the record on which to base approval of the requested
authorizations surrounding the merger.”).
18

19

 Finally, the Stipulation is in accordance with applicable New Mexico law and regulatory

principles.

        A.      Revenue Requirement

        SPS’s initial application sought an increase in revenue requirement of $175.3 million. The

Stipulation adjusted this revenue requirement increase down to $90.0 million, a reduction of close

to half of SPS's initial request. This is a substantial reduction and benefit to customers, and aligns

with the overall findings and recommendations made by various parties in this proceeding.20 The

agreed upon adjustments to the revenue requirement reasonably resolve the findings on SPS’s

retail cost of service and will provide SPS a reasonable opportunity to earn a fair overall rate of

return on the infrastructure used to provide service in New Mexico.

         B.      Capital Structure and Rate of Return

        The Stipulation’s ratemaking capital structure of 54.7% equity and 45.3% debt is

reasonable in combination with a stipulated Return On Equity (“ROE”) of 9.5%, compared to

SPS's initial request of 10.5% ROE. The stipulated overall rate of return was the result of

meaningful negotiations between the parties. Notably, the stipulated ROE of 9.5% was well within

the multiple ROE recommendations offered by various parties in this case, including FEA and

LES.21 The resulting overall rate of return of 7.59%, along with modifications to the Company’s

proposed depreciation rates discussed below, will support SPS’s credit metrics and its investment

grade bond rating, and will do so at reasonable rates to New Mexico customers.

        C.      Depreciation Rates and Service Life Extensions

        Section 1.2 of the Stipulation provides for adjustments to depreciation rates but does not

increase the revenue requirement in this case. The Stipulation accomplished this revenue neutral

result in part by extending the lives of various generating resources as outlined in Section 1.2 to

the Stipulation. Many parties viewed the extension of the service lives of Jones Units 1 and 2,

Nichols Units 1-3, Maddox Units 1 and 2, Plant X Unit 4, and Tolk Units 1 and 2 as reasonable.22

           D.      Direct Assignment of the Cunningham BESS

           The Stipulation reflects that the Cunningham BESS is primarily needed to meet New

Mexico’s environmental objectives but also provides New Mexico with accredited capacity

benefits. Hence, in developing a jurisdictional production capacity allocation, Cunningham BESS

will be directly assigned to New Mexico and the additional capacity needed to meet New Mexico’s

resource capacity will be allocated from the SPS system portfolio using the jurisdictional

production capacity allocator.24 However, the New Mexico coincident peaks will be reduced by

the Cunningham accredited capacity that is directly assigned to New Mexico.25 This methodology

ensures that New Mexico is not allocated system resource capacity costs that are in excess of the

system capacity needed to provide reliable service in New Mexico.26

           E.      Amortization Periods for Previously Approved Regulatory Assets and Debits

           Section 1.7 of the Stipulation develops a proposed amortization period for Excess Liability

Insurance (“ELI”) premiums, legacy meter costs, and community solar program costs. The

Stipulation also provides that SPS may earn a return on the Deferred Tax Asset (“DTA”) costs at

          G.         Revenue Allocation

          The stipulating parties agreed that it is appropriate to include Sagamore and Hale Wind

Generation as components of SPS’s generation resource portfolio. The stipulating parties agreed

to allocate the portfolio within the retail class cost of service using an Average and Excess Four

Coincident Peak (“A&E 4CP”) methodology that has been used in past rate cases to allocate SPS

resource portfolio costs.33 This approach aligns with well-established cost of service ratemaking

principles, which seek to assign costs to each rate class commensurate with their costs of service,

while applying the principle of gradualism to avoid rate shock.

          The Stipulation at Section 1.11 further provides that in developing the AED 4CP allocator,

a study will be performed to determine how behind the meter generation will be reflected in the

accurate measurement of production and transmission demand costs.

III.      Staff's Contested Issues

          Staff raised two challenges to the Stipulation regarding cost allocation, but both stem from

the key difference between Staff and the stipulating parties regarding the amount of revenue

deficiency that should be recovered in rates The Stipulation reflects an overall base revenue

increase of approximately 12.5%, while Staff recommended an overall base revenue increase of

approximately 6.7%.

          A.       Jurisdictional Cost Allocation.

           Staff's witness Dr. Blank mistakenly asserts a fundamental flaw in SPS's jurisdictional cost

allocation. Specifically, Dr. Blank asserts that SPS applies forecasted 12-CP and energy allocation

ratios in New Mexico while Texas and FERC do not employ the same forecasted methodology. 36

Dr. Blank ignores that SPS testified it uses a 12-CP basis for its jurisdictional allocation.37

          Dr. Blank also argues that because SPS projects significantly higher load growth in New

Mexico than in Texas, SPS’s use of a forecasted test period in New Mexico — while Texas uses a

historical base year — risks double recovery and an overstatement of the New Mexico revenue

requirement.38 Therefore, to correct this asymmetry, Dr. Blank recommends that the Commission,

for jurisdictional allocation purposes, requires SPS to use a base-year/Texas-consistent

37

 methodology, with adjustments limited to known and measurable changes. 39 Dr. Blank's

methodology, standing alone, reduces the revenue deficiency by approximately $56.7M.40

          Staff's position inexplicably ignores New Mexico law. New Mexico law expressly allows

for use of future test years while Texas law does not. The PUA provides:

          The commission shall set rates based on a test period that the commission
          determines best reflects the conditions to be experienced during the period when
          the rates determined by the commission take effect. If a future test period is
          proposed, the commission shall give due consideration that the future test period
          may best reflect those conditions.41

          Staff fails to explain how or why the Commission can ignore this statutory provision.

          During the hearing, Commission Chair O'Connell posed a somewhat related question to

testifying witnesses for signatories to the Stipulation regarding, from a customer point of view,

how to view fairness in a world where customers are going to be paying different rates in New

Mexico for the same thing that customers are paying for in Texas.42 Chair O'Connell made the

point that the same capital investment can get put into rate base in New Mexico under a future test

year sooner than the allocation to Texas under a historical test year, thus reducing regulatory lag

in New Mexico but not in Texas, and questioned whether that is fair.43

           SPS's witness Lees testified that, while it is true that New Mexico allows the use of future

test years in setting base rates where Texas does not, Texas does allow rate recovery of

infrastructure and other investments through a variety of rate rider cost recovery mechanisms,

starting on the date the infrastructure comes into service, and those costs are then rolled into base

rates with a true up in the next historic test year rate case.44 SPS witness Trowbridge also testified

that Texas has rate riders that bridge between the base rate test year and current rates, so they adjust

over time.45

          There is no evidence in this case that compares the proposed New Mexico stipulated base

rates with the Texas combined base rates plus rider rates for the same investments to demonstrate

that one jurisdiction's overall cost is higher or lower than the other's as a result of using a future

test year or due to the stipulated rates. However, SPS witness Trowbridge testified that, currently,

SPS's rates for its New Mexico customers are lower than its rates for its Texas customers, so the

presumption that New Mexico customers will always pay more than Texas customers due to New

Mexico's future test year does not hold.46

the renewable production resources from which the PTCs are generated are allocated based on the

ensure service reliability.
